item.title: Text Machines: Scarlet Thread of the Digital Order (1883-2026) at Green Library, Bing Wing
item.description: Stanford Libraries now holds an 1883 edition of a rare book, Les laboureurs: poème tiré de Jocelyn, whose pages (text and ornaments) were entirely woven on a Jacquard loom by the firm of silk merchant Joseph-Alphonse Henry. This exhibition explores the cultural contexts and material conditions of Les laboureurs’ production, and considers parallels between technology-driven global change in the late nineteenth century and in our current day. The exhibition includes microscope images revealing the textile structure of the woven text as well as a woven enlargement that illustrates its basic principles, along with several artworks inspired by or related to the themes of the exhibition.

item.title: A Vision of Paris: The Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford at Green Library, Bing Wing
item.description:
Stanford University Libraries presents A Vision of Paris: the Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford, on view in the Peterson Gallery and Munger Rotunda of the Cecil H. Green Library from September 22, 2026 to January 24, 2027. 

Roxane Debuisson (1927–2018) dedicated sixty years to documenting the transformation of the city of Paris during the nineteenth century.  If Roxane Debuisson could not stop the changes she saw underway in the late 20th century, she could at least preserve the city’s earlier history through images, literature, guidebooks, and other documents. 

Her lifelong project helped to document Paris during the nineteenth century, especially the city’s rapid changes from the 1850s to the 1870s, when Emperor Napoleon III and his prefect of the Seine, Baron Eugène Haussmann, transformed the city with new boulevards, green spaces, and public utilities, and fostered innovations in commercial and cultural practices. 

A Vision of Paris: the Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford draws upon the extensive array of commercial almanacs, prints, postcards, commercial ephemera, stereographs, manuscripts, historic photographs, and other items that are a part of the Roxane Debuisson Collection of Paris history, circa 1789-1970, acquired by the Department of Special Collections at Stanford University Libraries in 2020. These materials place Paris as the birthplace of political, commercial, and urban innovations, and as a city defined by the tension between its historical past and its continuous reinvention. The exhibit highlights the city’s rapid changes and their diverse causes, while suggesting the collection’s vast possibilities for both research and instruction.

This exhibition is curated by Sarah Sussman, Assistant University Librarian for Collections and Services & Curator of French and Italian Collections, Stanford University Libraries, and Chloe Summers Edmondson, Assistant Professor of French at the University of Miami. Produced and designed by Deardra Fuzzell, with assistance from Kylee Jo Diedrich, Sofia McGullam Ornelas, and Pasha Tope.

A Vision of Paris: the Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford will be open to the public. Registration at the entrance with a valid government ID is required to enter the Cecil H. Green Library and view the exhibit.

item.title: Electric Contrasts: the Art of the Detail at McMurtry Building
item.description:
Electric Contrasts: The Art of the Detail brings together photobooks and magazines to show how the revolution of photography in the late 19th and early 20th century changed the history of art. Electric Contrasts takes Kenneth Clark’s landmark 1938 book One Hundred Details from Pictures in the National Gallery as a starting point to illuminate the impact black and white photographic details of Old Master paintings had on new ways of seeing in the early 20th century. The exhibition reveals the anachronistic and provocative juxtapositions of artworks in avant-garde magazines and books which created a radically new vision that would go on to influence television and the internet.

Curated by Altair Brandon-Salmon. Bowes Art & Architecture Library hours: M-Th 9-7pm; Friday 9-5pm; Sunday 12-6pm.

item.title: Korean Indigenous Futures: The Art of Kim Bong-Jun 김봉준 판화전: 토착적 미래- K아트, 디아스포라, 세계 at Lathrop Library
item.description:
The East Asia Library at Stanford University will host a print exhibition by Kim Bong-Jun, a leading figure in Korean Minjung (People’s) Art, from September 29 to December 11, 2026. Active since the 1980s, Kim has developed a distinctive visual language that combines traditional Korean folk art and popular expression with contemporary art, reflecting the lives and realities of ordinary people and envisioning possibilities for a more just and ecological future. The exhibition explores Kim’s concept of “Indigenous Futures” through art as a form of civilizational transformation, expressing p'owŏl (포월 抱越), embracing and transcending the pain and contradictions of reality while reaching toward new possibilities for the future.

The opening reception on October 8 will feature an artist talk and a Korean mask dance (탈춤 t'alch'um) performance by Kim Bong-Jun and Che Se-hyun, a Seattle-based creative director and multidisciplinary artist.

The exhibition is curated by Jee-Young Park, Korean Studies Librarian, and Jisoo Kim, an SFSU MA Museum Studies graduate and San Francisco-based curator.

item.title: Evolving Approaches to Open Science and Research Transparency Education (Bay Area Open Science Group Meeting)
item.description:
This month we are joined by Jo Weech, Research Transparency Program Manager at the Berkeley Initiative for Transparency in the Social Sciences BITSS. Jo supports teams working on academic forecasting, evidence aggregation, and reporting in economics. In addition to its research projects, BITSS hosts an annual conference and course on research transparency. Her presentation for the September meeting will be on how education in open science and research transparency has evolved due to changes in researcher norms and use of AI.

About the Bay Area Open Science Group
The Bay Area Open Science Group is a growing community for Bay Area academics and researchers interested in incorporating open science into their research, teaching, and learning. Targeting students, faculty, and staff at UCSF, Berkeley, and Stanford, the goal of the community is to increase awareness of and engagement with all things open science, including open access articles, open research data, open source software, and open educational resources. Through this work the group hopes to connect researchers with tools they can use to make the products and process of science more equitable and reproducible.

item.title: Emergent Properties: Decennial Reflections on Collections at David Rumsey Map Center (Green Library)
item.description:
In 2026 the David Rumsey Map Center celebrates its tenth year—a moment to reflect on how the Center has added value to scholarship on campus and around the world. Our collections are vast and not bounded by geography, spanning the 15th century to the present. Yet over the last decade, certain materials have repeatedly resonated with the students, instructors, and researchers who frequent the Center. Emergent Properties brings together a selection of highlights from deep within the collections of the David Rumsey Map Center: items that have not only proven to be rare or beautiful, but have become the drivers of scholarship, programming, and support areas that have resonated with our users. The forty objects in this exhibition represent these emergent properties. Though only a glimpse into the full breadth of the Center’s holdings, they reflect what has mattered most over the past ten years. 

The exhibition will be on display at the David Rumsey Map Center within Green Library through Friday, March 5, 2027.

item.title: Wild & Bright: Designing for Belonging | Artist Talk with Yiying Lu, in Conversation with Thomas S. Mullaney
item.description:
What can a whale, a dumpling, and an endangered clouded leopard tell us about belonging?

Join artist and designer Yiying Lu, creator of Twitter’s Fail Whale and six emoji adopted into the Unicode Standard, for an opening talk celebrating Wild & Bright, an exhibition of nine large-scale digital paintings from her multi-year series on endangered species, on view in Hohbach Hall at Green Library through 2028.

Lu will trace the unexpected creative path connecting these seemingly different worlds: from a personal illustration that became Twitter’s Fail Whale in 2008, to emoji designed to expand the world’s shared visual vocabulary, to a red panda created for a Bay Area AAPI night market that opened an entirely new direction in her practice.

That exploration eventually led Lu to the United Nations Convention on Biological Diversity, where her logo design for COP15 received an Award of Honor, and to support from the Adobe Creative Residency Community Fund. Wild & Bright began on August 4, 2020, International Clouded Leopard Day, with the clouded leopard as the first animal in the series.

The work has since returned to the community in new ways. In 2025, sixteen pieces from the series were featured at a San Francisco Zoo fundraising gala, bringing art, storytelling, and wildlife conservation together.

Across Lu’s work runs a central question:

What does it take to make someone, or something, feel like it belongs in the picture?

She approaches belonging as a design inquiry: whether the subject is a species losing its natural habitat, a culture missing from a global visual language, or a whale that made failure feel unexpectedly human.

Following the presentation, Lu will join Professor Thomas S. Mullaney for a conversation about language, technology, and how visual systems decide who becomes visible. The program will conclude with an audience Q&A.

The event takes place in the lead-up to World Animal Day on October 4.

About Yiying Lu

Yiying Lu is an award-winning artist, designer, and creative leader working at the intersection of art, technology, culture, and human experience. For nearly two decades, her practice has moved across digital culture, brand systems, public art, creative technology, and civic life, translating complex ideas into visual experiences that connect across cultures and communities.

She is the creator of Twitter’s Fail Whale and has designed and successfully proposed six emoji adopted into the Unicode Standard, including the dumpling and boba tea. She previously served as Global Creative Director at 500 Global and as a San Francisco Arts Commissioner, appointed by the Mayor of San Francisco. She currently leads Happy Creative Land, a San Francisco-based innovation studio, and serves as an Adobe Global Creative Ambassador and a committee member of the UNESCO Chair in Digital Futures at Stanford.

Her creative collaborations have included Disney, Apple, Google, Airbnb, Adobe, and NYU Shanghai. She has spoken at SXSW, Web Summit, TEDx, Today at Apple, and Talks at Google, and her work has been featured in The New York Times, BBC, TIME, The Atlantic, WIRED, and The Wall Street Journal.

Lu has been recognized by Fast Company as one of its Most Creative People in Business, by Microsoft as a Top 10 Leader in Innovation, and by the Shorty Awards as its inaugural winner in Design.

Born in Shanghai, educated in Sydney and London, and based in San Francisco, Lu brings a lived global perspective to the ways design and storytelling can create connections across cultures, communities, and generations.

About Thomas Mullaney 

Thomas S. Mullaney is Professor of History and Professor of East Asian Languages and Cultures, by courtesy. He is also the Kluge Chair in Technology and Society at the Library of Congress, and a Guggenheim Fellow. 

He is the author or lead editor of 7 books, including The Chinese Typewriter (winner of the Fairbank prize), Your Computer is on Fire, Coming to Terms with the Nation: Ethnic Classification in Modern China, and the forthcoming The Chinese Computer—the first comprehensive history of Chinese-language computing.

His writings have appeared in the Journal of Asian Studies, Technology & Culture, Aeon, Foreign Affairs, and Foreign Policy, and his work has been featured in the LA Times, The Atlantic, the BBC, and in invited lectures at Google, Microsoft, Adobe, and more. He holds a PhD from Columbia University.

item.title: Google Earth Engine 101: The JavaScript Sandbox for Complete Beginners at Branner Earth Sciences Library
item.description:
Google Earth Engine 101: The JavaScript Sandbox for Complete Beginners

An Introduction to Satellite and Earth Observation Data for Beginners

Overview

This workshop provides a practical introduction to Google Earth Engine designed for members of the Stanford research and teaching community who are new to both satellite imagery and Earth observation data. The session emphasizes foundational concepts, hands-on exploration, and concrete examples that lower the barrier to working with large-scale geospatial data.

Google Earth Engine is a cloud-based geospatial processing platform that combines a multi-petabyte catalog of satellite imagery and geospatial datasets with planetary-scale analysis capabilities. It enables users to explore environmental change, map patterns, and compute statistics across large spatial and temporal extents—without the need to download or locally store massive datasets.

Instructor

Stace Maples

Note: This workshop is open to Stanford University affiliates only.

Session Description

The Earth Engine API allows users to write custom algorithms for processing raster and vector data directly in the cloud. This workshop is geared toward participants who want to understand how satellite imagery and related datasets are structured, accessed, and analyzed using Earth Engine.

The session will be hands-on and will use the Earth Engine JavaScript Code Editor throughout.

Workshop Structure

  • Part 1: A Tiny Introduction to Remote Sensing
    An accessible introduction to satellite and Earth observation imagery, including fundamentals of the data model, spectral characteristics, spatial and temporal resolution.

  • Part 2: Working in Google Earth Engine
    Practical instruction on:

    • Navigating the Earth Engine interface
    • Accessing and filtering imagery collections
    • Creating image composites
    • Running analyses over image stacks
    • Computing summary statistics
    • Generating charts
    • Exporting analysis results

Prerequisites

No prior experience with Google Earth Engine or JavaScript is required.
However:

- Familiarity with GIS or remote sensing concepts is helpful
- Prior programming experience is beneficial but not required
- A willingness to learn basic programming concepts is essential 

Accessing Google Earth Engine

Many Stanford affiliates already have access to Google Earth Engine through the Stanford Geospatial Center’s collaboration with the Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability.

To check your access: 1. Visit: https://code.earthengine.google.com/f983a2d843739e23ffb77f336ad6d4fb
2. Log in using your Stanford.edu credentials
3. If successful, the script will generate a Tanaka hillshade visualization of terrain in Yosemite Valley

If you do not have access, email maples@stanford.edu to request inclusion in the Stanford Geospatial Center’s organizational Earth Engine account.

Access can only be provided to users with valid Stanford.edu credentials and a fully sponsored SUNet ID.

Slides

The slides used in this workshop mirror those presented during the live session and can be opened in a separate window for reference, including embedded links.

https://slides.com/staceymaples/gee101/embed

Sample Scripts

After receiving confirmation of your Earth Engine account, you may import the sample script repository used in this workshop. These scripts are designed to introduce the basic mechanics of working in Google Earth Engine and can be explored and modified at your own pace.

https://goo.gl/9f9NgB

item.title: Text as data: Using Redivis and AI to analyze historical news sentiment
item.description:
This hands-on workshop introduces social scientists to Redivis as a platform for text-based research, using an AI-powered sentiment analysis task as a working example. Participants will use Redivis's no-code transform interface to prepare a real dataset of historical newspaper coverage using a subset of the Library of Congress's Chronicling America collection, then run a guided Python notebook that applies a modern language model to measure shifts in tone over time. This is a practical, applied session focused on building and running a real analysis pipeline. No prior programming experience is required, though some familiarity with Python will be helpful.

Speaker Adelynn Shirts is a member of the Redivis team, where she works directly with researchers and organizations to support their use of data for research and analysis. Her work spans research support, data workflows, technical documentation and education resources, with a focus on helping researchers use Redivis effectively for data preparation, analysis and reproducible research.

She holds both a a bachelor’s degree in Sociology and master’s degree in Data Analytics from Utah State University, with her master’s studies through the Department of Mathematics and Statistics focused on statistics, machine learning, and data science.

item.title: Planetscope Satellite Imagery 101: Real-Time Satellite Monitoring for Research at Branner Earth Sciences Library
item.description:
Real-Time Satellite Monitoring with Planetscope Imagery

Using PlanetScope Imagery for Research and Teaching at Stanford

Overview

This workshop introduces Planet.com and its PlanetScope daily imagery, with a focus on practical workflows for discovering, accessing, and analyzing high-resolution satellite data for academic research and instruction.

With a constellation of roughly 200 Dove satellites in orbit, PlanetScope provides near-global coverage of the Earth at approximately 3.7-meter spatial resolution, refreshed daily. These data support time-series analysis, environmental monitoring, land-use change detection, and other applications where temporal frequency is critical. Access is available through Planet’s web applications, APIs, and GIS integrations.

Audience

This session is designed for members of the Stanford research and teaching community who are interested in using PlanetScope imagery at scale. No prior experience with Planet tools or APIs is required, though familiarity with GIS, remote sensing, or Python will be helpful.

Attendance is limited to current Stanford University affiliates with full SUNetID privileges.

Agenda

Introduction to Planet and PlanetScope

  • Overview of Planet’s satellite constellations
  • PlanetScope daily imagery characteristics and use cases
  • Access models for academic users at Stanford

Searching and Accessing Imagery with Planet Explorer

  • Navigating the Planet Explorer web interface
  • Defining areas of interest and time ranges
  • Filtering imagery by date, cloud cover, and other attributes
  • Previewing scenes and understanding data products

Programmatic Access with the Planet APIs

  • Overview of the Planet Data and Orders APIs
  • Authentication and basic API concepts
  • Transitioning from interactive search to automated workflows

Hands-On Walkthrough Using a Python Notebook

  • Guided walkthrough of the provided Jupyter Notebook 
  • Demonstration of searching for PlanetScope imagery via the API
  • Submitting and managing orders programmatically 
  • Using Planet’s server-side processing tools 
  • Downloading and visualizing imagery 

The notebook emphasizes clarity and transparency over optimization, making it appropriate as both a learning tool and a starting point for custom research pipelines.

Logistics

Participants who wish to follow along should bring their own laptops. Computers will not be provided.

PlanetScope Access at Stanford

Stanford provides institutionally supported access to PlanetScope imagery for research and teaching. Details on eligibility, access procedures, and data use guidance are available here:

https://guides.library.stanford.edu/c.php?g=1013467&p=10216495

item.title: Community Mapping Prejudice Session: Transform Historic Racial Covenants into Actionable Data
item.description:
• Location: Virtual (Zoom link provided upon registration)
  • Date and Time: 10:00-11:30AM, Friday, October 16, 2026
  • Lead Instructor: Zoe Dilles (Map Librarian)

Join us for a community mapping session where we will identify racially restrictive covenants in property deeds in Contra Costa County, California and become part of a nation-wide, crowd-sourced community mapping project with more than 14,000 participants! 

What is a racially restrictive covenant?

This is discriminatory language included in historic land and property documents to prevent non-White property ownership and residency. Covenants were used in every US state in the 20th century to segregate communities on the basis of race and ethnicity. 

What will we do in this workshop?

We will help identify racially restrictive language in scanned primary source documents and contribute to the University of Minnesota Mapping Prejudice project. In accordance with California law, counties must "proactively identify and redact unlawfully restrictive language that may be found in the public record." You will receive step-by-step support in the processs of transcribing information from historic property records so that it can be mapped and made into actionable data.

Details:

  • Please register to attend online over Zoom.
  • Open to all Stanford University community members. 
  • Sign up for a free Zooniverse account to participate.
  • No prior mapping experience needed. 

Not a Stanford affiliate or can't make it to this session? Join a public online community mapping session through the University of Minnesota!

item.title: Foxes and Lions: Renaissance City-States in the Age of Machiavelli at Green Library, Bing Wing
item.description:
Join the Silicon Valley Archives in welcoming cultural historian Paul Wright to discuss his forthcoming board game from GMT Games, Foxes and Lions: Renaissance City-States in the Age of Machiavelli, on Wednesday, October 21st at 4pm.

Foxes and Lions (co-designed with Liz Davidson) is a richly historical “sandbox game” in the same series as GMT’s Here I Stand, Virgin Queen, and Tanto Monta—each of which covers a different aspect of 15th or 16th century Europe. While most games in the series have a broader canvas, Foxes and Lions focuses specifically on the Italian Wars during the period 1494-1527, both in Italy proper and in the Venetian colonies of the Balkans; this is the period stretching from the rise of Friar Savonarola to the notorious Sack of Rome. Five players take on the roles of five key political protagonists identified by Machiavelli in The Prince—the Republic of Venice, the Duchy of Milan, the Republic of Florence, the Kingdom of Naples, and the Papacy.

In part, the game exists to put the emphasis on Italian experiences of the Italian Wars, an emphasis lacking in most wargames on the period, which often devolve into narratives of “greater powers” like France and Spain. In Foxes and Lions, players are fundamentally underdogs in a precarious environment, and while strenuously competing with one another, they must also beware of non-player antagonists among the “great powers” of the era, which include France, Spain, the Holy Roman Empire, and the Ottoman Empire. In fact, players may even lose collectively to the great powers and find “Italian virtù” exhausted by external threats, much as Machiavelli had warned throughout his writings—and what was arguably the ultimate outcome of the historical conflicts.

Foxes and Lions also promises to be the first board game to honor the full range and dynamism of Machiavelli’s writings, including the Discourses on Livy, Florentine Histories, The Art of War, and more. The game also includes the colorful, talented, and controversial condottieri—the captains independently contracted to lead various powers’ troops and their own mercenaries. In this light, the game interrogates (rather than simply accepts) Machiavelli’s condemnation of mercenaries and their captains, bound as that was to his celebration of citizen militias as preferable alternatives for both their patriotism and their capacity for instilling civic virtues, especially in republics. The game also explores the role of diverse political systems in the Italian political sphere (including merchant republics, princedoms, feudal aristocracies, and theocracies), as well as how Machiavelli’s ideas about popular sentiment reflect his deeper concerns with the precarity of all political arrangements.

In his talk, Wright will explore the decade-long genesis of Foxes and Lions as a product of a career dedicated to teaching and researching Machiavelli, as well as the inspiration afforded the game by scholars ranging from John Pocock to Albert Ascoli, John Najemy, Anthony Grafton, and many others. He will also discuss how the game navigates the difficult yet essential space somewhere between historical simulation and ludic sandbox that allows for counterfactual outcomes. He will also address the broader role of game-based learning and games as historical inquiry, as well as how these growing traditions have shaped the evolution of Foxes and Lions.

item.title: Book Event with Kimberley Johnson and Pedro Regalado: "Dark Concrete: Black Power Urbanism and the American Metropolis" at Green Library, Bing Wing
item.description:
Please join the Silicon Valley Archives in welcoming Kimberley Johnson and Pedro Regalado as they discuss Johnson's latest book, Dark Concrete: Black Power, Urbanism, and the American Metropolis, on October 22, 2026, at 4:30 p.m. This event is co-sponsored with the Silicon Valley Archives by the Program on Urban Studies at Stanford, the Stanford Department of African and African American Studies, the Stanford Program in American Studies, and the Stanford Center for Comparative Studies in Race and Ethnicity. 

Please RSVP at this link to attend. 

Dark Concrete is about how the Black Power movement reshaped urban politics in the United States—from expectations to practices. Although the national and international dimensions of the Black Power movement are often focused on, Kimberley Johnson looks at the movement at the local level, highlighting Newark and East Orange, New Jersey, and Oakland and East Palo Alto, California, and three policy areas: housing, education, and policing. She examines how Black Power Urbanism had its own local meanings as it was defined by local activists, neighborhood residents, parents, tenants, and others who sought to repair cities and particularly black neighborhoods that were shattered due to urban renewal and highway construction, as well as ongoing political and economic disinvestment. Dark Concrete depicts how local conditions influenced the emergence of the Black Power movement and, in turn, the ways in which these local movements reshaped urban politics, institutions, and place.

Kimberley S. Johnson is Professor of Social and Cultural Analysis at New York University, with affiliate appointments in the Department of Politics and the Wagner Graduate School of Public Service. Johnson recently held the John G. Winant Visiting Professorship in American Government at the University of Oxford (2024-25). Johnson’s work examines American political development, the formation of the modern administrative state and bureaucratic governance; urban and suburban governance; race and ethnic politics; and the political production of (sub-)urban space.

Pedro A. Regalado is an Assistant Professor of History at Stanford University. Regalado's work focuses on cities, immigration, capitalism, and empire, with particular attention to Latino communities. He is especially interested in how everyday working people, migrants, and entrepreneurs shaped, and were shaped by, the political economy of urban America across the twentieth century.

    • Zach Lannes (Engineering Librarian for Research & Teaching Support)
    • Alex Threlkeld (Mathematics, Statistics & Computational Sciences Librarian)
    • Jooyeon Hahm (Head of Data Science Training & Consultation)

This workshop is an introduction to programming in Python for people with little or no previous programming experience who want to use Python for data analysis and visualization. Working entirely within Jupyter notebooks via Google Colab, learners progress from the absolute fundamentals—running code, assigning variables, understanding data types and type conversion, and calling built-in functions and help—through importing and using libraries from Python's standard library and beyond. The course then centers on real-world data work using the Pandas library and the Gapminder global development dataset, teaching learners to read tabular CSV data into DataFrames, inspect and summarize it, and create plots with matplotlib. Later episodes build core programming skills including lists, for loops, conditionals, looping over data sets, and writing functions, with scheduled coffee and lunch breaks structuring a full-day, hands-on format reinforced throughout by practice challenges and reflection exercises.

Please register to attend. Registration is open exclusively to current Stanford affiliates and is offered on a first-come, first-served basis. In-person attendees should bring their Stanford ID or a valid government-issued ID for library access, along with their laptop. Virtual attendees will receive a Zoom link upon registration.

item.title: The Illicit Finance Hydra: Crypto, Sanctions Evasion, and the New Financial Battlefield at Hohbach Hall
item.description:
Join the Stanford University Libraries on Tuesday, October 27, 2026 from 5:30 -6:30 pm for a presentation by Alexander Browder on crypto-based money laundering activity across the globe, spanning 164 cases and 20 years.

Event Description

Cryptocurrency is rapidly reshaping illicit finance and the enforcement of international sanctions. Alexander Browder, founder of the Global Cryptocurrency Laundering Database, will discuss what he learned from analyzing major cases spanning two decades, including the growing use of digital assets and stablecoins by Russia, Iran, North Korea, and other illicit actors. He will explore how crypto networks can enable sanctions evasion, state-backed activity, and money laundering, and what governments, financial institutions, and technology companies can do in response. Browder will also discuss how his research resulted in the UK, EU and other countries addressing this emerging threat, and ultimately led to him being sanctioned by the Russian government in June 2026.

Speaker Biography

Alexander Browder is a financial-crime researcher and founder of the Global Cryptocurrency Laundering Database (launderingdatabase.org), the first and largest open-source global database focused on cryptocurrency laundering. He is the author of “Confronting the Illicit Finance Hydra in Crypto Markets”, published by the Henry Jackson Society in March 2026. He is an associate fellow at the HJS and a research associate at the Yale Chief Executive Leadership Institute. Browder has presented his research in the UK and EU Parliaments, advised policymakers on sanctions and illicit finance, and have been interviewed by news organisations around the world. In June 2026, Russia placed him on its entry-ban list following his work investigating Russian cryptocurrency-based sanctions evasion activity.

This event is free and open to the public, but registration is required in advance. Please visit the RSVP Form to register.

item.title: Two Views of the Chinese Coast at David Rumsey Map Center (Green Library)
item.description:
Join us for "Two Views of the Chinese Coast," a talk by Kären Wigen, the Frances & Charles Field Professor in Stanford's Department of History, at the David Rumsey Map Center. When cartographic collections began to appear online in the 1990s, historians of East Asia were quick to seize on maps as subjects for research. Over the next thirty years, a sophisticated field of critical map studies developed, illuminating the lively landscape of cartographic production across the early modern Sinosphere. While map-focused research made rapid strides, a gap gradually opened between cartographic research (the history of maps) and what we might call map-informed history (history with maps). 

This talk attempts to address that gap by investigating two works from Stanford University Libraries’ collections: a Qing-era scroll painting of the Pacific coast, housed in the David Rumsey Map Collection, and a British map of the same shoreline from 1859, owned by a private collector and held digitally within the Barry Lawrence Ruderman Map Collection. During the 19th century, both maps served as tools of military planning; where the Qing scroll was likely consulted for coastal defense, the British chart was designed for a naval attack. By putting them in dialogue with each other, the talk suggests how cross-cultural map comparison can help us tell more complex, entangled stories about Euro-Asian interaction.

Speaker Bio

Kären Wigen teaches Japanese history and the history of cartography. A geographer by training, she earned her doctorate at the University of California at Berkeley. Her first book, The Making of a Japanese Periphery, 1750-1920 (1995), mapped the economic transformation of southern Nagano Prefecture during the heyday of the silk industry. Her second book, A Malleable Map: Geographies of Restoration in Central Japan, 1600-1912 (2010), returned to the ground of that study, exploring the roles of cartography, chorography, and regionalism in the making of modern Shinano.  An abiding interest in world history led her to co-author The Myth of Continents (1997) with Martin Lewis. She also introduced a forum on oceans in history for the American Historical Review and co-edited Seascapes: Maritime Histories, Littoral Cultures, and Transoceanic Exchanges (2007) with Jerry Bentley and Renate Bridenthal. Her latest book is Territorial Imaginaries: Beyond the Sovereign Map (2025).

Event details

This event is available to attend in-person or remotely via livestream. Please register to attend the event in-person as seating is limited. The livestream link will be posted on this page at a later date and will also be emailed to subscribers of the David Rumsey Map Center email newsletter.

item.title: Book Event with Roland Betancourt and T.L. Taylor, "Disneyland and the Rise of Automation" at Green Library, Bing Wing
item.description:
Please join the Silicon Valley Archives in welcoming Roland Betancourt and T.L. Taylor as they discuss Betancourt's latest book, Disneyland and Rise of Automation, on December 2, 2026, at 4:30 p.m. 

 

Disneyland and the Rise of Automation argues that theme park rides are factory assembly lines in disguise, ones that manufacture subjects rather than products. The book traces the technological systems that made this possible, from limit switches and relay racks to programmable logic controllers and magnetic tape, revealing how innovations developed for wartime manufacturing and Cold War industry found new life in the Happiest Place on Earth. It applies insights from the history of technology to problems shared by historians, media scholars, and critics of visual culture, such as the aesthetics of automation and the politics of labor.

  

Roland Betancourt is a Chancellor’s Professor at the University of California, Irvine. He is currently the Andrew W. Mellon Professor at the Center for Advanced Study in the Visual Arts at the National Gallery of Art. A 2023 Guggenheim Fellow, he has published books on Byzantine visual culture, gender, and sexuality, including the prize-winning Byzantine Intersectionality (Princeton, 2020).

 

T.L. Taylor is Professor of Comparative Media Studies at MITand affiliate faculty member in Anthropology and Women’s and Gender Studies. She is a qualitative sociologist who has focused on the interrelations between culture and technology in online environments for over thirty years. Her work sits at the intersection of sociology, media studies, and science and technology studies.
